candidates.title: A Controlled Generative Model for Segmentation of Liver Tumors
candidates.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a generative model representing the formation of liver CT images and employ it for segmentation of hepatic tumors. We extend the graphical model used in label fusion techniques for the segmentation of multi-modality Magnetic Resonance brain images. To resemble atlas data, we segment the first slice by a physician and propagate it for processing of subsequent slices. We include a knowledge-based constraint in the model that is considered as a key difference with classical generative models. We compared our method with conventional Bayesian techniques and state-of-the-art hepatic tumor segmentation algorithms. We achieved a measure of 0.86 ± 0.06 and 0.76 ± 0.09 regarding Dice and Jaccard metrics respectively that is better than recent researches.

candidates.title: Automatic segmentation and classification of the liver tumor using deep learning algorithms
candidates.abstract: Liver tumors are one of the life-threatening cancers with the fastest-growth rates worldwide. Early detection of tumors may therefore reduce morbidity and increase the survival rate. The development of automated techniques for the precise segmentation of hepatic tumors is essential for assisting doctors in tumor diagnosis and preoperative planning for surgical treatment of the liver which reduces the risk of surgical resection. The classification and segmentation of hepatic tumors in Computerized Tomography (CT) scan pose a great challenge due to noise, unclear boundaries, heterogeneity, and variability in tumor tissue appearance, shape, size, and location. In this study, we describe a novel method for automatic segmentation and classification of hepatic tumors in CT scan images using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks. For tumor segmentation, we created a modified Dense U-net model. The classification framework is based on a novel deep CNN with a pre-trained VGG-16 network to distinguish between normal and malignant liver tumors. The proposed system was evaluated based on MICCAI 2017 Liver Tumor Segmentation (LiTS) Challenge dataset and obtained the best result with a Dice Score of 95.40%, Jaccard Index of 92%, and accuracy of 92.60% for segmentation and the classification model has achieved an accuracy of 96%, Sensitivity of 95.80%, Specificity of 96.20% and Precision of 95.80%.

candidates.title: Automatic liver tumor segmentation from CT scans with knowledge-based constraints
candidates.abstract: Automatic hepatic tumor segmentation is a crucial step for diagnosis and surgery planning. This paper presents a new fully automatic technique to segment the tumors in liver structure with no interaction from user. Contrast enhancement is applied to the slices of segmented liver, then adding each image to itself to have a white image with some pepper noise and tumors as dark gray spots. After applying Gaussian smoothing, Isodata is used to threshold the tumor in the slice. In order to eliminate erroneous segmentation, discriminative rule based on diagnostic knowledge on liver cancer shape is applied along with a 3-D consistency check is performed based on three-dimensional information that a lesion mass cannot appear in a single slice independently. Tests are performed on 9 abdominal datasets and promising result shows that sensitivity and specificity for automatic liver tumor segmentation are 87% and 99% respectively.

candidates.title: Comparison of two‐dimensional and three‐dimensional iterative watershed segmentation methods in hepatic tumor volumetrics
candidates.abstract: In this work the authors compare the accuracy of two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) implementations of a computer-aided image segmentation method to that of physician observers (using manual outlining) for volume measurements of liver tumors visualized with diagnostic contrast-enhanced and PET/CT-based non-contrast-enhanced (PET-CT) CT scans. The method assessed is a hybridization of the watershed method using observer-set markers with a gradient vector flow approach. This method is known as the iterative watershed segmentation (IWS) method. Initial assessments are performed using software phantoms that model a range of tumor shapes, noise levels, and noise qualities. IWS is then applied to CT image sets of patients with identified hepatic tumors and compared to the physicians' manual outlines on the same tumors. The repeatability of the physicians' measurements is also assessed. IWS utilizes multiple levels of segmentation performed with the use of "fuzzy regions" that could be considered part of a selected tumor. In phantom studies, the outermost volume outline for level 1 (called level 1_1 consisting of inner region plus fuzzy region) was generally the most accurate. For in vivo studies, the level 1_1 and the second outermost outline for level 2 (called level 2_2 consisting of inner region plus two fuzzy regions) typically had the smallest percent error values when compared to physician observer volume estimates. Our data indicate that allowing the operator to choose the "best result" level iteration outline from all generated outlines would likely give the more accurate volume for a given tumor rather than automatically choosing a particular level iteration outline. The preliminary in vivo results indicate that 2D-IWS is likely to be more accurate than 3D-IWS in relation to the observer volume estimates.

candidates.title: Procesamiento de imágenes médicas mediante conjuntos neutrosóficos
candidates.abstract: El procesamiento de imágenes médicas constituye un área crítica para el diagnóstico, donde la incertidumbre y la ambigüedad inherentes a los datos biomédicos limitan la efectividad de los métodos convencionales. En este contexto, la teoría neutrosófica ha emergido como un marco matemático robusto para el manejo explícito de información imprecisa. Este artículo de revisión presenta un análisis del estado del arte en procesamiento de imágenes médicas mediante conjuntos neutrosóficos, abarcando sus fundamentos teóricos, las principales técnicas de preprocesamiento, segmentación y extracción de características, y su integración con modelos de inteligencia artificial y aprendizaje profundo. Asimismo, se examinan comparativamente sus ventajas frente a los métodos clásicos basados en lógica difusa, así como sus limitaciones actuales relacionadas con la escalabilidad, la automatización y la integración en flujos clínicos digitales. Finalmente, se discuten los retos y oportunidades futuras, destacando el potencial de la neutrosofía híbrida y explicable como herramienta clave para el desarrollo de sistemas médicos más precisos, interpretables y confiables en la medicina de precisión contemporánea.

candidates.title: Advances in Deep Learning and Image Processing for Brain Tumor Detection and Classification: A Comprehensive Review
candidates.abstract: Brain tumor identification and classification by the application of deep learning and sophisticated image-processing techniques have been receiving a lot of attention in the medical field. Accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcome rely on the accurate identification and differentiation of brain tumors, such as gliomas, meningiomas, and metastases. The most recent developments in deep learning-based techniques for brain tumor identification and categorization by applying medical imaging data, including Computed Tomography (CT). This study looks at CT and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). The main topic of this study is the general theory and developments in deep learning methods for the identification and classification of brain tumors. It investigates how the precision and efficacy of tumor detection can be increased through a variety of models, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The paper emphasizes the Significance of applying novel deep-learning techniques for facilitating precise and automated brain tumor identification for individualized treatment, with an emphasis on important achievements, challenges, and opportunities in the area.

candidates.title: Robots for CT-guided needle insertion: clinical implementation and future perspectives
candidates.abstract: Robotic systems for computed tomography (CT)-guided needle insertion have been developed to address the limitations of conventional manual needle insertion. Thus far, various robotic systems have been clinically implemented, and accumulating evidence has suggested their clinical utility. The evidence has evolved beyond initial feasibility and early clinical experience to include larger observational and comparative studies. These studies have demonstrated high success rates of robot-assisted needle insertion in various CT-guided interventions, including thermal ablation, biopsy, and preoperative localization. Furthermore, an increasing number of comparative studies have demonstrated the advantages of robot-assisted procedures over conventional manual procedures. These advantages include improved needle insertion accuracy and reduced radiation doses to patients and/or physicians. Although most currently available robotic systems are needle-guiding robots designed to align a needle guide with a predetermined insertion trajectory, we have developed a CT-guided needle insertion robot capable of robotic needle advancement via remote control. Clinical studies have demonstrated the feasibility of robotic needle insertion using this system, as well as needle placement accuracy comparable to that of manual procedures, while eliminating radiation exposure to physicians. The integration of artificial intelligence and the implementation of telerobotic interventions are expected to contribute significantly to the further advancement of robotic systems for CT-guided needle insertion. This narrative review summarizes the current clinical implementations and available evidence for robotic systems for CT-guided needle insertion, including our system, and discusses future perspectives in this field.

candidates.title: Comprehensive motion management for liver SBRT on a 1.5 T MR-Linac: Initial clinical experience and dosimetric comparison with an ITV-based workflow
candidates.abstract: Background and purpose Respiratory-gated MR-guided workflows enable expiration-gated liver stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) based on real-time intrafraction target monitoring. We evaluated the dosimetric impact and early clinical feasibility of this approach by comparing clinically delivered expiration-gated plans with retrospectively generated non-gated ITV-based plans. Methods The first 20 consecutive patients treated with online adaptive MR-guided SBRT for primary or secondary liver malignancies on a 1.5 T MR-Linac between October 2024 and April 2025 were included. Five patients had two lesions, treated with separate plans in two patients, resulting in 22 matched plan pairs. For each clinically delivered gated plan, a retrospective ITV-based plan with identical prescription dose was generated. Paired differences were tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and p -values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The dose–volume analysis was considered exploratory. Results Median planning target volume was lower with the gated workflow than with ITV-based planning (28.0 vs. 41.9 cc). Organ-at-risk constraint violations were fewer with the gated workflow (10 vs. 19), with 11 violations resolved and 2 newly occurring. PTV D98% did not differ significantly ( p = 0.41), although one gated and four ITV-based plans showed PTV D98% < 95%. Uninvolved liver dose was significantly lower with the gated workflow (median Dmean difference 0.97 Gy and 0.93 Gy for three- and five-fraction plans; adjusted p ≤ 0.037). Among 93 evaluable fractions, the mean plan-level median active delivery time was 7.6 min for three-fraction and 6.7 min for five-fraction treatments. Conclusion Expiration-gated MR-guided liver SBRT reduced target volumes and improved normal tissue sparing without compromising target coverage or routine clinical feasibility.

candidates.title: Reviewer #2 (Public review): An Itch Receptor Drives Melanoma
candidates.abstract: Mas-Related GPCR X4 (MRGPRX4) is a sensory neuron-restricted receptor for cholestatic itch. Here, we identify MRGPRX4 as an unexpected melanoma driver. MRGPRX4 is upregulated in melanoma and is confined to invasive, neural-crest-like and pre-EMT states associated with dedifferentiation and therapy resistance. Ectopic MRGPRX4 expression in mouse melanocytes drives 100% penetrant, highly metastatic melanoma, demonstrating oncogenic behavior. MRGPRX4 promotes melanoma cell proliferation and invasion through basal, ligand-independent, PI3K-AKT-MAPK activation. Multi-omics links MRGPRX4 expression to a mesenchymal/neural-crest–like program that defines a distinct invasive MRGPRX4+ niche. Comparing transcptomics of MRGPRX4-driven tumors shows a broad overlap with BRAF/NRAS-driven tumors; however, the MRGPRX4 model also enriches an ECM-rich, invasive neural crest–like melanoma state. MRGPRX4 further remodels the tumor microenvironment toward an immunosuppressive, checkpoint-high state enriched in suppressive myeloid cells. Pharmacologic MRGPRX4 inhibition suppresses basal signaling and limits melanoma growth and invasion. In sum, melanoma exploits MRGPRX4 to acquire an invasive and immunosuppressive phenotype, nominating this somatosensory GPCR as a promising therapeutic target.

candidates.title: WavPAC-Net: a wavelet-based hybrid encoder network with permuted axial-channel feature enhancement for liver segmentation
candidates.abstract: The liver, core to human metabolism and detoxification, is threatened by chronic diseases like cirrhosis that increase hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, with early diagnosis dependent on accurate liver segmentation in medical imaging. Current clinical segmentation methods generally suffer from low efficiency, strong subjectivity, and scarcity of AI-driven commercial products. Although deep learning technologies have been applied to liver segmentation, mainstream architectures still exhibit inherent limitations: CNN struggles with long-range dependencies while Transformer lacks fine detail representation. This study proposes WavPAC-Net, an innovative wavelet-based fusion network incorporating: (1) a hybrid CNN-Transformer encoder combining ConvNeXt-Small branch for precise hepatic parenchymal texture capture and Swin Transformer branch for long-range dependency modeling; (2) a Wavelet Domain Fusion Module (WDFM) that decomposes the features extracted by CNN and Transformer into low-frequency and high-frequency sub-bands respectively, and performs adaptive weighted fusion; and (3) a Permuted Axial-Channel Feature Enhancer (PACFE) that implements cross-dimensional refinement of high-dimensional fused features through collaborative three-dimensional spatial modeling and channel dimension permutation. In systematic comparisons with 20 state-of-the-art segmentation models, WavPAC-Net demonstrates statistically significant advantages in both segmentation accuracy and boundary fidelity. Evaluated on the CirrMRI600+ dataset (T2-weighted MRI), WavPAC-Net achieved Dice score of 93.16%, IoU of 88.45%, and MCC of 93.03%, with a computational complexity of 19.88 GFLOPs. Multi-modal validation on the public LiTS CT dataset further confirmed the model’s excellent performance, achieving Dice score of 96.91%, IoU of 94.32%, and MCC of 96.79%. Overall, WavPAC-Net provides an effective balance between segmentation accuracy and computational complexity, supporting its potential for practical liver segmentation applications.

candidates.title: Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI deep learning model combined with clinical model for noninvasive differentiation of hepatocellular carcinoma from mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
candidates.abstract: Rationale and objectives This study aims to develop a framework integrating dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI)-based multi-channel deep learning combined with clinical modeling for the non-invasive preoperative discrimination between hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (MF-ICC). Methods The internal development cohort comprised 334 surgically confirmed patients, including 231 patients with HCC and 103 with MF-ICC, and was divided at the patient level into a training cohort ( n = 233) and an internal validation cohort ( n = 101). The independent external validation cohort included 50 patients, comprising 40 with HCC and 10 with MF-ICC. We constructed separate two-dimensional deep learning models based on arterial phase, portal venous phase, and delayed phase images and then developed fusion models (2D model). A multi-channel deep learning model was further developed by directly inputting the three-phase images stacked along the channel dimension. Moreover, a clinical model was built based on independent predictors identified through multivariate analysis, which was ultimately integrated with the best-performing deep learning model. Model performance was evaluated and compared. Results Deep learning model directly feeding the three-phase images as a multi-channel input achieved better discrimination (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.814 in the internal validation cohort) than all single-phase and corresponding fusion models. The comprehensive 2D + multi-channel + clinical model showed the best performance for the differentiation of HCC from MF-ICC, achieving an AUC of 0.887 (95% CI, 0.819–0.954) in the internal validation cohort, and generalized well to the external validation cohort (AUC = 0.908; 95% CI, 0.811–1.000). However, no significant differences in AUCs were found among the models after correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusion The fusion model integrating clinical predictors with DCE-MRI multi-phase deep learning feature may provide a valuable tool for preoperatively differentiating HCC from MF-ICC.
